principle_name: Services Are Sold on Trust Not Features
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: When the prospect is evaluating MOTM like a commodity — comparing on price, asking for feature lists, or demanding guarantees before engaging.
when_not_to_use: When the relationship is already established and the prospect is in proposal or negotiation stage.
principle: Professional services are credence goods — the buyer cannot evaluate quality before purchase and must trust the provider. They are sold on relationships, referrals, and reputation, not on attributes, features, or price comparisons. When a prospect asks about features or price before trust is established, they are using the wrong evaluation framework — and the rep's job is to shift the frame.
questions_to_ask: Have you worked with an outsourced sales partner before?
What would a successful outcome look like for your business in 12 months?
Who do you currently trust to advise you on your sales strategy?
recommended_action: Shift the conversation away from features and price toward relationships, track record, and reputation. Never respond to a features-based objection with more features — respond with proof of outcomes and trust signals.
what_not_to_do: Do not send a detailed service brochure or capability deck in response to a pricing objection. Do not defend price with a longer list of deliverables. Do not compare MOTM to competitors on features — that is the wrong battleground for a trust-based service.
motm_application: When a prospect asks what MOTM does or why they should pay this much, do not pitch the service list. Instead establish credibility through case outcomes and the MOTM track record. The question to answer is not what do you do but what has happened for companies like mine when they worked with you.

principle_name: The Seven Elements — The Client Buying Journey for Professional Services
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: When diagnosing why a BD opportunity is stuck at any stage. Use as a diagnostic framework before choosing any tactic — the correct intervention depends entirely on which element is failing.
when_not_to_use: This is a diagnostic lens not a tactical script. Do not recite the seven elements to a prospect. Use it internally to identify where the relationship is breaking down.
principle: Before a client buys a professional service they must satisfy seven sequential conditions: (1) Aware — they know you exist, (2) Understand — they know clearly what you do, (3) Interested — what you do is relevant to their current goals, (4) Respect — they believe you can deliver, (5) Trust — they believe you have their best interests at heart, (6) Able — they have budget and authority, (7) Ready — the timing is right internally. A breakdown at any single element stops the sale regardless of strength in others.
questions_to_ask: Do they know MOTM exists?
Do they understand clearly what MOTM does and for whom?
Is what MOTM does relevant to their current priorities?
Do they believe MOTM can deliver — do we have proof?
Do they trust that MOTM has their interests at heart?
Do they have budget and authority to decide?
Is the timing right internally right now?
recommended_action: Before deciding on any tactic, map the prospect against all seven elements and identify the weakest one. The intervention must target that specific element. Do not jump to closing if trust has not been established. Do not keep pitching if the real issue is ability or readiness.
what_not_to_do: Do not send another proposal when the real problem is the prospect does not have internal buy-in. Do not offer a discount when the real problem is the prospect does not yet believe MOTM can deliver. Do not keep following up without diagnosing which element is actually stuck.
motm_application: When a MOTM BD conversation stalls, map the prospect against these seven elements before deciding on the next move. A prospect who likes MOTM but keeps delaying is usually stuck at Element 6 (Ability — no budget or authority) or Element 7 (Readiness — wrong timing) — not at trust or interest. The intervention is to help them build the internal case, not to pitch harder or discount.

principle_name: Build Awareness Before You Attempt to Sell
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
chapter: Chapter 9 - Element 1: I Am Aware of You
when_to_use: When approaching a completely cold prospect who has no prior exposure to MOTM, or when planning a BD outreach strategy for a new industry or geography.
when_not_to_use: When the prospect already knows MOTM — focus then shifts to understanding and interest elements. Do not invest awareness-building effort in prospects who already know you.
principle: A prospect cannot buy from someone they have never heard of. Awareness must be built before any selling attempt. The most effective awareness-building in professional services is narrowcasting — being very well known to a small, defined group of the right people — rather than broadcasting to large audiences. Knowing 200 of the right people well outperforms being vaguely known to 20,000.
questions_to_ask: Has this prospect ever heard of MOTM?
Is there a shared connection who could introduce us?
What industry event, publication, or community does this prospect pay attention to?
Who in our existing network could provide a warm introduction?
recommended_action: Define the exact company type and decision maker profile MOTM wants to serve. Build systematic, consistent awareness with that specific group through relevant contact — articles, introductions, events, referrals — before any selling attempt. Aim to be known to the right 100-200 people very well rather than vaguely known to thousands.
what_not_to_do: Do not cold-pitch a prospect who has never heard of MOTM and expect them to engage with a commercial proposal. Do not invest in mass marketing when the target is a small number of high-value companies. Do not try to sell before the prospect is even aware you exist.
motm_application: MOTM BD should define the exact company type and decision maker profile — for example, MDs of Indian industrial manufacturers in the ₹50-250 Cr range — and invest in becoming well known in that narrow group through consistent, relevant contact before attempting to sell. Attending the right industry events, publishing relevant content, and leveraging referrals from existing clients are more effective than cold outreach at scale.

principle_name: Shrink the Pond — Niche Positioning Dominates in Professional Services
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
chapter: Chapter 10 - Element 2: I Understand What You Do
when_to_use: When a prospect says they do not understand exactly what MOTM does, or when MOTM is being compared against generic alternatives, cheaper options, or hiring internally.
when_not_to_use: When the prospect already has a clear understanding of MOTM's positioning and differentiation.
principle: Being undifferentiated in professional services is fatal. A firm must niche itself so clearly that prospects immediately know what it does, who it serves, and how it is different. The smaller and more specific the niche claim, the more likely prospects are to remember the firm when they have that specific need. Being the largest, first, or best in a small, defined pond beats being average in a large ocean. Specificity attracts — vagueness repels.
questions_to_ask: What specific type of company does MOTM serve best?
What is the one problem MOTM solves better than any alternative?
How can MOTM claim to be first, best, or most experienced in a specific category?
Can we describe our niche in one sentence that a stranger could repeat?
recommended_action: MOTM BD must be able to state in one sentence what MOTM does, who it serves, and how it is different. The positioning must mention a specific niche — type of company, size, industry, or problem — not a generic we help companies grow sales. Shrink the target definition until MOTM can claim a clear leadership position within it.
what_not_to_do: Do not pitch MOTM as a company that helps all businesses with all their sales needs — too broad to be memorable. Do not try to compete across every segment simultaneously. Do not describe MOTM with generic language like sales outsourcing or BD support — these mean nothing to a busy MD.
motm_application: MOTM should not pitch itself as a general sales outsourcing company. The positioning should be specific — for example: We help Indian industrial manufacturers in the ₹50-500 Cr range build structured sales execution without the cost and risk of hiring in-house. This niche positioning is memorable, referable, and immediately relevant to the right prospect.

principle_name: The Four-Component Elevator Pitch — Niche, Who, How, Different
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
chapter: Chapter 10 - Element 2: I Understand What You Do
when_to_use: When preparing any first introduction of MOTM — cold call opener, LinkedIn message, first meeting introduction, or email subject line. The elevator pitch must be ready before any outreach begins.
when_not_to_use: In deep discovery conversations where listening is more important than pitching. Do not recite the elevator pitch when the prospect is already asking questions — that is a signal to listen and engage, not to continue presenting.
principle: A strong professional services pitch has exactly four components: (1) A statement of your niche — what specific space you occupy, (2) A statement of who you serve — the specific type of client, (3) A statement of how you help — the outcome you produce, (4) A statement of how you are different — what no one else does. Without all four, prospects cannot understand or remember you — and they will not refer you to others. The pitch must be repeatable by someone who just heard it once.
questions_to_ask: What is MOTM's niche in one phrase?
Who specifically does MOTM serve — what type of company and decision maker?
What specific outcome does MOTM produce for clients?
What makes MOTM different from hiring a salesperson or using a different BD agency?
recommended_action: Build a single crisp MOTM elevator pitch using all four components and use it consistently across all BD outreach. Test it by asking whether a stranger who just heard it could repeat it accurately to a colleague. If not, simplify until they can.
what_not_to_do: Do not use jargon or long service lists in the elevator pitch. Do not describe inputs and activities — describe the outcome. Do not use a different pitch every time — consistency builds recognition. Do not confuse listing services with explaining value.
motm_application: A strong MOTM elevator pitch: MOTM is an outsourced sales execution partner for Indian industrial manufacturers. We help companies in the ₹50-500 Cr range build and run structured sales teams without the cost and risk of hiring in-house — delivering pipeline, qualified meetings, and revenue growth through embedded sales engineers. One sentence. Covers all four components. Repeatable.

principle_name: Interest Is Created by Relevance to Their Goals — Not by Your Service List
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: In first meetings and discovery conversations when a prospect seems politely interested but is not actively engaging or showing urgency. This is the most common stall point in BD conversations.
when_not_to_use: When the prospect has already expressed clear interest and urgency — do not slow down with more discovery when the prospect is ready to move forward.
principle: A prospect becomes interested only when they can see how what you do is directly relevant to their specific goals and priorities right now. Interest is not created by explaining your services — it is created by demonstrating that you understand their situation and that your work will have a meaningful impact on what they are trying to achieve. If what you offer is not relevant to their current priority, they will not engage regardless of how good your pitch is. You must connect your capability to their goal before interest exists.
questions_to_ask: Could you share what your main revenue or growth priorities are for this year?
What is the one sales challenge that is costing you the most right now?
How are you being measured this year — and how is sales execution connected to that?
What would need to change in your sales performance for you to consider this year a success?
recommended_action: Before pitching, ask about current business priorities. Then connect MOTM explicitly to a specific goal the prospect has just stated — not to a generic business problem. The connection must be direct: this goal, this obstacle, this is how MOTM removes that obstacle, this is what that means for the goal.
what_not_to_do: Do not pitch the full MOTM service catalogue to a prospect without first understanding what they are specifically trying to achieve. Do not assume the problem you solve is the same one they are thinking about. Do not talk about MOTM features when the prospect has not yet confirmed they have the relevant goal.
motm_application: Do not pitch MOTM as a solution to a generic sales problem. Connect it to what this specific company is trying to achieve. If they are entering a new market, MOTM is the fastest way to build sales presence without permanent headcount. If they are trying to grow key accounts, MOTM provides the structured account management their team lacks. Relevance is built through their goal, not through MOTM's service list.

principle_name: When a Prospect Is Not Interested — Ask for a Referral Before You Leave
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: When a prospect has clearly confirmed they do not have a current need for MOTM and the conversation is coming to an end. This is the single highest-ROI action available in a no-opportunity meeting.
when_not_to_use: Do not ask for a referral before the prospect understands what MOTM does — they cannot refer something they cannot explain to someone else.
principle: If a prospect genuinely does not have a need that matches your services, do not walk away empty-handed. A referral from a known contact carries instant trust and collapses the awareness and trust stages of the buying journey for the referred prospect. One referral from a credible source is worth more than ten cold approaches. Always ask before leaving a no-opportunity meeting.
questions_to_ask: I completely understand — this might not be the right time for you. Would you happen to know anyone else who is dealing with this kind of sales challenge?
We work best with companies in your kind of space that are trying to grow their sales team without full-time hires. Does anyone in your network come to mind?
Would you mind if I mentioned your name when I reach out to them?
recommended_action: Before ending any no-opportunity conversation, ask explicitly for a referral. Name the type of company and situation you are looking for to make it easy for the prospect to identify someone. Be specific — not anyone who needs sales help but a ₹50-200 Cr manufacturer trying to grow their sales pipeline without hiring a full team.
what_not_to_do: Do not end a no-opportunity conversation with thanks and goodbye — this leaves the most valuable BD output unused. Do not ask for a referral in a way that feels like a desperation move — ask naturally, as a practical next step. Do not ask for a referral before the prospect knows what MOTM does well enough to explain it to someone else.
motm_application: No MOTM BD conversation should end without asking for at least one referral if there is no direct opportunity. This is a low-effort, high-return habit that compounds over time. One referral per week from no-opportunity meetings alone can build a significant warm pipeline within six months.

principle_name: Track Record Is the Only Credible Proof in Professional Services
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
chapter: Chapter 12 - Element 4: I Respect Your Work
when_to_use: Whenever a prospect asks about MOTM experience or capability, or when they show hesitation about whether MOTM can actually deliver. The credibility question is always implicit even when not asked directly.
when_not_to_use: Do not lead with case studies before understanding the prospect's specific situation — the case must be highly relevant to resonate. An irrelevant case study damages credibility.
principle: In professional services, past performance is the only fact-based way to evaluate a provider. Prospects ask have you done this before and what happened more than any other question. Credentials, presentations, and promises are words — case studies with specific, quantified outcomes are evidence. The more similar the reference case is to the prospect's situation, the more powerful it is. Specific always beats general.
questions_to_ask: Would it be helpful if I shared how we handled a similar situation for a company like yours?
What specific outcome would give you confidence that MOTM can deliver for you?
What has your experience been with other vendors or approaches to this challenge?
recommended_action: Have 3-5 MOTM case studies ready that match the type of company and challenge of the current prospect. Always lead with the most relevant case — same industry, similar size, similar challenge. Quantify the outcome: pipeline generated, meetings set, revenue closed, time to productivity. Never use a generic success story when a relevant one exists.
what_not_to_do: Do not share a generic MOTM success story about a different industry or company size — irrelevant cases damage credibility. Do not describe what MOTM did without describing what the outcome was. Do not claim outcomes you cannot support with evidence. Do not lead with credentials before demonstrating understanding of the prospect's situation.
motm_application: The MOTM case library must be built and continuously maintained. For every BD conversation, identify the most relevant MOTM case and lead with it specifically — not a general description of capabilities. The structure is always: company like yours, same challenge, here is what we did, here is the specific outcome. This format is more convincing than any credential or feature list.

principle_name: Trust Has Two Components — Competence and Good Intentions
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: In early relationship stages and whenever a prospect expresses concern about whether MOTM will actually act in their interests. The second dimension of trust — good intentions — is often the harder one to establish and the more decisive one.
when_not_to_use: Do not fake client-first behaviour as a tactic — prospects can detect insincerity over time and it destroys the relationship permanently. This only works when it is genuine.
principle: Trust in professional services has two components. The first is competence-trust: will they get the job done? This is built through credentials, track record, and demonstrated expertise. The second is benevolence-trust: will they do the right thing by me? This is built through consistent client-first behaviour — sharing bad news quickly, admitting mistakes, not recommending unnecessary work, and sometimes declining business that is not a good fit. The second component is often the deciding factor because it is harder to fake and harder to verify.
questions_to_ask: Before we go further, can I ask — what would make you feel this partnership is genuinely working in your interest?
Are there any concerns about how this would actually work that I should address directly?
What has your experience been with vendors who did not have your best interests at heart?
recommended_action: Demonstrate client-first behaviour in every BD interaction. If during discovery it becomes clear that MOTM is not the right solution for this company right now, say so honestly. This single act of honesty builds more trust than any pitch — and often leads to a referral or a future opportunity when the situation changes.
what_not_to_do: Do not push a prospect to sign a contract when it is clear their situation does not match what MOTM delivers — this destroys trust at the first delivery milestone. Do not withhold concerns or limitations to avoid losing the deal. Do not prioritise closing over fit — a poor fit engagement damages the MOTM reputation more than a lost deal.
motm_application: If BD discovery reveals MOTM is not the right solution for this company right now, say so directly. This is the most powerful trust-building act available — and it demonstrates exactly the client-first orientation that makes future prospects trust MOTM when the fit is right. McKinsey's most cited trust story is a partner who turned down a signed engagement because they were not the right firm for that specific project.

principle_name: Trust Is Accumulated One Transaction at a Time Over Time
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: When a BD conversation is moving slowly and the prospect is not ready to commit. Use this principle to frame a long-term relationship-building approach rather than a short-term closing mindset.
when_not_to_use: Do not use this as an excuse to avoid asking for a decision when the time is clearly right — there is a meaningful difference between patience and passivity.
principle: Trust in professional services is not built in a single meeting or a single proposal — it accumulates through repeated positive interactions over time. Each small act adds to the trust account: responding quickly, following through on a small commitment, sharing a useful insight, making a genuinely helpful introduction. The longer the trust history, the lower the risk perception and the easier the purchase decision becomes. Patience in trust-building is not weakness — it is the correct strategy for high-value professional services.
questions_to_ask: What would be most useful for me to share with you right now even if we are not working together yet?
Is there anyone in your network I could introduce you to who might be helpful to you?
What is the most useful thing I could send you this month to stay relevant to what you are working on?
recommended_action: When a prospect is not ready, do not push or disappear. Continue adding value through consistent, lightweight contact — relevant industry insights, useful case examples, thoughtful introductions, occasional check-ins with something genuinely useful. The goal is to be the most trusted option when internal conditions change.
what_not_to_do: Do not send repeated just following up messages to a prospect who is not ready — this depletes the trust account rather than building it. Do not disappear from prospects who are not yet ready. Do not let patience become inactivity — stay proximate with genuine value.
motm_application: MOTM BD should treat every prospect relationship as a long-term investment. A prospect who is not ready now but is in the right type of company is worth consistent nurturing. Consistent valuable contact — not just follow-up calls asking for decisions — builds the trust account that converts when the timing is right. The standard should be one genuinely useful contact per month minimum for warm prospects.

principle_name: Referrals Are the Most Powerful and Underused BD Tool in Professional Services
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: After any successful MOTM engagement or milestone — and systematically at the end of every engagement phase as a standard process step, not an afterthought.
when_not_to_use: Do not ask for referrals before delivering genuine value — a referral from an unsatisfied or uncertain client is worse than no referral.
principle: Clients in professional services hire people they know, respect, and trust — or who come highly recommended by someone they know, respect, and trust. A referral from a trusted contact collapses the awareness, understanding, and trust stages of the buying journey in a single introduction — turning a cold prospect into a warm one immediately. It is the fastest and most cost-effective BD method available. Most professional services firms report that the majority of their best clients came through referrals — yet most firms do not systematically ask for them.
questions_to_ask: We have really enjoyed working with you on this — if you feel we have done a good job, would you mind introducing us to one or two other companies that might benefit from a similar outcome?
We work best with companies in the ₹50-250 Cr range in industrial manufacturing. Does anyone in your network come to mind?
Would you be comfortable making a brief introduction over WhatsApp or email?
recommended_action: After every successful MOTM engagement milestone, ask explicitly who else in the client network might benefit. Be specific about the type of company to make it easy for the client to identify someone. Make it easy for them to refer — offer to draft the introduction message for them.
what_not_to_do: Do not complete a successful engagement and never ask for a referral. Do not make the referral request feel like a sales ask — frame it as connecting people who could genuinely benefit. Do not ask for referrals to anyone — be specific about the type of company you are looking for so the client can think of the right person.
motm_application: MOTM BD must systematically harvest referrals from every satisfied client as a standard step in the engagement process — not an occasional ask. Every client relationship should produce at least one warm introduction to a similar company. One referral per client per year compounds into the most valuable BD pipeline MOTM can build.

principle_name: Find the Right Person With Budget and Authority — The Magic Formula
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: When a BD conversation is progressing but it is unclear whether the person being spoken to has the authority and budget to make a decision. This must be clarified early — not discovered after months of investment.
when_not_to_use: Do not eliminate a contact just because they lack obvious authority — they may be the path to the right person and could become a valuable internal champion.
principle: A prospect cannot buy from you if they lack the authority to decide or the budget to commit. The magic formula is: High ROI proposition plus the right level of stakeholder equals ability to engage. However, ruthlessly pre-qualifying out everyone who lacks obvious budget is a mistake — the right question is under what conditions would this prospect be able to act not can they buy today. In complex organisations, the decision is rarely made by one person — identify the full stakeholder group.
questions_to_ask: For a decision like this, who else would typically be involved in the conversation?
Do you have a budget allocated for sales capability investment this year?
If we put together a proposal, who would need to review and approve it?
Is there a budget cycle or planning review coming up where this could be considered?
recommended_action: Ask early and directly whether the contact has authority over this type of decision. If not, ask to meet the person who does — or ask for the current contact to advocate internally. Understand the budget cycle and decision process before investing significant BD effort. Map the full stakeholder group before submitting a proposal.
what_not_to_do: Do not invest three months of BD effort with a Sales Head who has no authority to approve an external engagement without MD sign-off. Do not assume the most enthusiastic person in the room is the decision maker. Do not send a proposal without first confirming who all the approvers are.
motm_application: MOTM BD should quickly identify whether the contact has authority to approve a sales outsourcing engagement — typically MD, CEO, or Founder level. If not, work with the current contact to access the right decision maker. A Sales Head who is enthusiastic about MOTM but cannot approve the engagement is a champion — not the buyer. Treat them accordingly and focus on equipping them to sell internally.

principle_name: Build a Specific ROI Case — Vague Benefits Do Not Create Ability to Buy
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: When a prospect is interested but keeps delaying or says they need to think — this often means they cannot yet justify the investment internally. A specific ROI case gives them the language and numbers to sell the decision internally.
when_not_to_use: Do not present an ROI case before understanding the prospect's specific numbers and goals — generic ROI claims are unconvincing. Build the ROI case from their own numbers, not industry averages.
principle: Clients need to justify a professional services investment both to themselves and to their organisation. They cannot approve a spend they cannot explain. A high ROI proposition — specific, quantified, and tied to the prospect's own goals and numbers — is what gives them the ability to act. Vague benefits do not create ability to buy. The prospect must be able to walk into their next internal meeting and explain why this investment makes financial sense.
questions_to_ask: What is the revenue target your sales team is responsible for this year?
What does it cost you to hire, train, and retain a senior salesperson all-in including recruitment, salary, benefits, and management time?
If you were to generate X additional qualified meetings per month, what would that be worth in pipeline?
What is the cost to your business of not solving this problem — in revenue terms?
recommended_action: Build a specific ROI comparison based on the prospect's own numbers — cost of hiring vs MOTM cost, expected pipeline impact based on comparable cases, revenue opportunity at risk if nothing changes. Present it in a format the prospect can use to brief their internal stakeholders. Make the numbers conservative and evidence-based — aggressive ROI claims invite scrutiny and skepticism.
what_not_to_do: Do not respond to a price objection by listing all the things MOTM does — this does not address the need to justify the investment with a number. Do not use industry average ROI figures — use the prospect's own context. Do not present an ROI case with assumptions the prospect cannot verify.
motm_application: MOTM BD must be able to build a specific ROI comparison for every prospect — comparing the full cost of hiring one or more salespeople against the MOTM retainer, and projecting pipeline impact based on comparable MOTM cases. The comparison should always show that hiring is more expensive, slower to productivity, and higher risk than MOTM. When the prospect says MOTM is expensive, the answer is always: compared to what?

principle_name: Not Ready Is Not No — Stay Proximate Until Timing Is Right
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: When a prospect has expressed genuine interest but delays repeatedly citing internal reasons — budget cycle, reorganisation, other priorities, leadership changes. This is the most common reason good prospects do not convert in the expected timeframe.
when_not_to_use: Do not confuse not ready with not interested — if a prospect has clearly confirmed no interest, staying proximate wastes BD effort. Read the signal correctly before applying this principle.
principle: A prospect can have full awareness, understanding, interest, respect, trust, and ability — and still not buy because the timing is not right internally. Budget cycles, reorganisations, leadership changes, and competing priorities all affect readiness. Not ready is not no. The professional who is most proximate when the timing does become right wins the engagement — because the trust was built during the waiting period, not at the moment of decision.
questions_to_ask: When do you think would be the right time to revisit this?
Is there anything I can help you with in the meantime — even if we are not working together yet?
What would need to change internally for this to become a priority?
What is the trigger event that would make this the right time?
recommended_action: When a prospect is not ready, do not push or disappear. Move them to a deliberate nurture track with consistent, lightweight contact — one genuinely useful touchpoint per month minimum. Stay close enough that when the internal conditions change, MOTM is the first call they make.
what_not_to_do: Do not mark a not-right-now prospect as lost and stop contact. Do not send repeated follow-up messages asking for a decision — this creates pressure without value. Do not disappear from warm prospects because they are not moving at your pace. Do not interpret internal delays as signals of disinterest.
motm_application: A MOTM prospect who says not right now should be moved to a structured nurture track — not abandoned and not pushed. The MOTM BD pipeline should have a nurture category for prospects who are interested but not yet ready, with a monthly contact plan delivering genuine value. The goal is to be the most trusted, most proximate option when their internal conditions change.

principle_name: Never Say Sell — The BD Mindset That Wins in Professional Services
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: As a foundational mindset principle for every BD conversation. The way a BD person thinks about their role in a conversation determines the quality of that conversation more than any tactic or technique.
when_not_to_use: This is a mindset principle — it does not replace the need to ask for a decision when the time is clearly right. Client-first does not mean avoiding commercial conversations.
principle: The best rainmakers in professional services do not think of what they do as selling. They think of BD as identifying a community of companies they can genuinely help and then doing everything possible to be of service — sharing insights, making introductions, asking good questions, being genuinely useful. The commercial relationship is the natural outcome of genuine service, not the goal of a sales process. The moment a BD conversation is driven by the seller's need to close rather than the prospect's need to solve a problem, the quality of the conversation collapses.
questions_to_ask: What is the biggest sales or growth challenge you are dealing with right now?
What have you already tried and why did it not work as expected?
What would the ideal outcome look like for you if you got the right support?
What would make this conversation genuinely useful to you today?
recommended_action: Approach every BD conversation with a single guiding question: is MOTM genuinely the right solution for this specific company right now? If yes, explain how. If no, say so. The goal is to be the trusted advisor who is the first call when a need arises — not to close every conversation into a contract.
what_not_to_do: Do not open every BD conversation by explaining MOTM services and pushing for a proposal. Do not treat every prospect as a revenue opportunity to be converted — treat them as a person with a specific challenge you may or may not be able to help with. Do not let the need to close override the need to understand.
motm_application: MOTM BD should approach every conversation with the mindset: let me understand their situation and see if MOTM is genuinely the right solution. This produces better conversations, higher trust, better fit engagements, and ultimately more conversions than a push-to-close approach — because prospects can always feel whether someone is trying to help them or trying to sell to them.

principle_name: MOTM Is an Optimizing Service — The Prospect Does Not Have to Buy It
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
chapter: Chapter 16 - A Chain Is as Strong as Its Weakest Link
when_to_use: When designing the BD approach for a prospect who is not in obvious pain and does not have an urgent immediate need — which describes the majority of MOTM BD prospects.
when_not_to_use: When the prospect already has a burning platform — urgent pipeline crisis, new market they must enter immediately — in that case urgency is self-evident and this framing is less relevant.
principle: Professional services fall into three categories: evergreen (recurring services like accounting), acute (emergency response like crisis management), and optimizing (discretionary improvement). MOTM is an optimizing service — the prospect can choose not to engage and survive. This means the prospect has no inherent urgency to act and no automatic budget for the service. The only way to convert an optimizing service sale is to connect the service directly to a specific goal the prospect has already committed to and show it is the fastest or most cost-effective path to that goal.
questions_to_ask: What growth target have you committed to for this year or next?
Is there a specific market or customer segment you have been trying to crack that is not moving fast enough?
If your sales pipeline is not where it needs to be, what is the annual revenue cost of that gap?
What is the plan if your current approach to sales continues producing the same results next year?
recommended_action: Never position MOTM as a general improvement or a nice-to-have. Always connect it to a specific urgent goal the prospect has already committed to — a revenue target they have told their board, a new market they have announced, a growth plan that requires pipeline. The framing must be: you have already committed to this goal, MOTM is the fastest way to get there.
what_not_to_do: Do not pitch MOTM to a prospect who is comfortable with current performance and has no committed growth target — they have no reason to change. Do not position MOTM as something worth considering eventually — connect it to something they have already decided to pursue. Do not lead with MOTM's capabilities before establishing the prospect's own committed goal.
motm_application: MOTM BD must find and amplify the prospect's own urgent committed goal and show that MOTM is the fastest, most cost-effective way to achieve it. A personal trainer gets hired when someone has committed to a specific goal — a reunion, a health target, a marathon. MOTM gets hired when a company has committed to a specific revenue target they cannot achieve with their current sales approach.

principle_name: Great Delivery Is the Highest Form of BD — Quality Produces Referrals and Renewals
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: As a foundational principle for how MOTM prioritises delivery quality. Especially relevant when a BD person is tempted to over-promise to close a sale — because the promise made today determines the referral or churn that results in 90 days.
when_not_to_use: This is a long-term principle — it does not replace the need for active BD effort in the short term. Great delivery does not automatically produce new business without deliberate BD activity alongside it.
principle: In professional services, the product and the person cannot be separated. You are the product. The quality of delivery is the foundation of reputation, referrals, and repeat business — which are the three primary sources of new business for successful professional services firms. Great work travels by word-of-mouth faster than any marketing effort. One exceptional first engagement produces more future business than six months of cold outreach.
questions_to_ask: Before closing, are we confident we can deliver what we are promising for this specific client?
What does success look like for the client in the first 90 days — and are we set up to deliver it?
Have we committed to anything in the sales process that delivery cannot honour?
recommended_action: Never close a sale with commitments delivery cannot honour. Invest in making every first engagement exceptional — it is the highest-ROI BD action available. Before any engagement begins, align internally on what success looks like and how MOTM will deliver it for this specific client.
what_not_to_do: Do not over-promise to close a deal and then underdeliver — this destroys the reputation that took months of BD effort to build. Do not treat delivery as separate from BD — delivery outcomes are the foundation of the next BD cycle. Do not accept engagements that are clearly a poor fit just to close a deal.
motm_application: Every MOTM sales engineer placed with a client is either a BD asset or a BD liability. An SE who delivers exceptional results produces referrals, renewals, and case studies that power the next ten BD conversations. An SE who underdelivers ends that client relationship and closes off the referral network that client represented. Delivery quality is not separate from BD — it is the most important BD investment MOTM makes.

principle_name: Persistence Is a Non-Negotiable Characteristic of Successful BD
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: When a prospect has gone cold, not responded, or is delaying — and when building the right expectations about what BD in professional services actually looks like over time.
when_not_to_use: Do not confuse persistence with pestering. Every contact must add genuine value — persistence without value just creates noise and eventually annoyance. Quantity of contacts without quality of content is not persistence, it is harassment.
principle: BD in professional services requires extraordinary persistence because the sales cycle is long, most prospects are not ready when first approached, and genuine rejection is far less common than timing-based delays. The professionals who build the strongest practices are those who treat each no or not now as information rather than rejection and continue building the relationship over time. Giving up after two or three attempts is the single most common BD failure mode.
questions_to_ask: Have we genuinely given up too early on this prospect?
What is the most valuable thing we could share with this prospect right now to stay relevant?
Have we tried multiple different channels and approaches — or just repeated the same one?
What is a genuine reason to reach out to this person this month?
recommended_action: Plan a systematic contact cadence across different channels — call, email, WhatsApp, LinkedIn — each delivering something genuinely useful. Commit to staying in contact for at least 6-12 months before reassessing a warm prospect. Each contact should have a specific reason that is relevant to the prospect right now — not just a follow-up.
what_not_to_do: Do not send repeated just following up or just checking in messages — these are low-value contacts that train the prospect to ignore you. Do not disappear from a prospect after two attempts. Do not interpret a non-response as a definitive no — most non-responses in professional services are timing issues, not rejections.
motm_application: MOTM BD should expect a typical prospect relationship to require 6-18 months of consistent nurturing before converting — this is normal for professional services at this price point. Build a pipeline large enough that long cycles do not create pressure to close prematurely. One warm follow-up per month with a genuine reason to reach out is more effective than five generic check-ins.

principle_name: All Business Is Personal — Face to Face Builds Trust Faster Than Any Digital Channel
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: When planning a BD strategy for a new geographic market or high-value prospect segment — and when deciding how to allocate BD time between in-person and digital activities.
when_not_to_use: For early-stage awareness building and low-priority nurture contacts, digital communication is efficient and appropriate. Reserve in-person investment for high-value prospects and critical relationship moments.
principle: Despite the prevalence of digital tools, professional services clients still prefer to meet and engage face-to-face before making significant purchasing decisions. Trust is built faster and more durably through in-person interaction than through any digital equivalent — because human beings assess each other through multiple sensory channels simultaneously that video and messaging cannot replicate. The most successful professional services firms consistently invest in being physically proximate to their target clients.
questions_to_ask: When did we last meet this prospect in person?
Is there an industry event, conference, or exhibition where we could meet this prospect face-to-face?
Have we invited this prospect to visit MOTM or meet the team in person?
Is there a reason to be in their city this month that we could use to arrange a meeting?
recommended_action: Prioritise in-person meetings for first meetings, proposal presentations, and key relationship-building moments. Use digital communication — WhatsApp, email, LinkedIn — for nurturing between in-person contacts and for low-priority prospects. Budget for travel to key prospect locations for high-value accounts.
what_not_to_do: Do not run an entire BD process for a major engagement over email and video calls — and then lose to a competitor who invested in in-person visits. Do not treat digital convenience as equivalent to in-person relationship quality. Do not skip the in-person first meeting because it requires travel — the investment is consistently worth it for high-value accounts.
motm_application: MOTM BD should invest in face-to-face meetings with high-value prospects — especially for first meetings and commercial proposal presentations. Digital follow-up supplements personal contact but cannot replace it for high-value relationship development. The BD person who visits a prospect's factory and understands their operation in person has a fundamental trust advantage over one who has only ever sent emails.

principle_name: Always Be Listening — Questions Create More Interest Than Any Pitch
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: In every BD meeting — especially first and second meetings where the temptation is to fill the time explaining MOTM capabilities. The insight that the prospect shares in response to good questions is the most valuable BD content available.
when_not_to_use: Do not over-ask questions if the prospect is clearly impatient and has asked for a specific recommendation — read the room. Some prospects want a consultant's recommendation, not an interview. Match the questioning approach to the prospect's style.
principle: In professional services BD, the ratio of listening to speaking should favour listening heavily — especially in first and second meetings. Asking good questions about the prospect's goals, challenges, and priorities creates more genuine interest than any pitch. Questions signal expertise, demonstrate genuine interest in the prospect's situation, and reveal the specific need that the pitch must address. Always Be Listening replaces Always Be Closing in professional services.
questions_to_ask: Could you share your main commercial priorities for this year?
What has your experience been with building or managing a sales team so far?
What would you describe as your biggest obstacle to reaching your revenue targets?
If you were to engage an external partner, what would success look like in the first six months?
What have you tried before and what did not work the way you expected?
recommended_action: Limit the MOTM pitch to a maximum of 10 minutes in a first meeting. After that, ask questions. Use the prospect's answers to guide which MOTM capability to emphasise. The pitch must be responsive to what they just said — not a pre-scripted presentation delivered regardless of their answers.
what_not_to_do: Do not spend 40 minutes explaining MOTM services in detail in a first meeting and learn nothing about what the prospect actually needs. Do not ask questions as a performance — ask them because the answers genuinely matter to what you recommend. Do not pivot immediately from listening to pitching — let the prospect's answers settle before responding.
motm_application: MOTM BD should approach every first meeting with a list of discovery questions — not a rehearsed MOTM presentation. The prospect's answers reveal the specific need; the MOTM pitch is then tailored specifically to that need. A meeting where the prospect talks for 60% of the time and leaves feeling understood is far more likely to convert than a meeting where the BD person presented for 60% of the time.

principle_name: BD Must Be a Daily Discipline — Not an Episodic Crisis Response
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: When evaluating MOTM BD activity levels and building the right habits for the BD team. The feast-or-famine cycle is one of the most damaging patterns in professional services and is directly caused by episodic BD.
when_not_to_use: This is a process principle — it does not provide tactical guidance for specific prospect situations.
principle: Most professionals do BD in bursts — when work is slow they fire up the BD machine, land projects, get busy, stop doing BD, and then find themselves in a pipeline drought again. Successful rainmakers make BD a consistent daily or weekly practice regardless of delivery workload. The trust and relationship compounding that produces the best new business takes years to build — and is destroyed by periods of disappearance. Episodic BD creates a feast-or-famine cycle that is commercially damaging and psychologically exhausting.
questions_to_ask: How many hours per week are we currently dedicating to BD activity?
What is in the pipeline right now that was seeded 6-12 months ago?
Are we doing BD only when we are worried about pipeline — or as a consistent discipline regardless of current workload?
What would our pipeline look like in 12 months if we maintained consistent BD activity from today?
recommended_action: Dedicate a specific protected block of time every week to BD activity — regardless of delivery workload. This weekly BD time should include: prospect outreach, existing client contact for referrals, follow-up on warm prospects, and content or insights to share. Treat BD time as non-negotiable, not as something that happens when there is spare time.
what_not_to_do: Do not allow delivery pressure to eliminate BD activity entirely for weeks or months at a time. Do not treat BD as something that happens only when the pipeline is thin. Do not allow the team to oscillate between all-delivery and all-BD — maintain both simultaneously at a sustainable level.
motm_application: MOTM must build a culture where BD is a consistent weekly discipline — not something that happens when there is time or when the pipeline is thin. Delivery and BD must be maintained simultaneously. The compounding value of relationships built over 12 months of consistent contact cannot be replicated by an intensive BD sprint when the pipeline is empty.

principle_name: The Capability Deck — Send a High Quality Follow-Up Within 24 Hours
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
chapter: Chapter 12 - Element 4: I Respect Your Work
when_to_use: After any first BD conversation where the prospect has asked for more information or indicated genuine interest. The speed and quality of the follow-up deck is a direct signal of MOTM's professionalism and capability.
when_not_to_use: Do not send a generic capability deck unsolicited as a cold outreach tool — it reads as spam. Only send after a conversation where interest has been expressed and the prospect has asked for something in writing.
principle: After a first BD conversation, a prospect commonly asks for something in writing — a deck, a summary, something they can review and share with colleagues. This request is a test: how quickly do you respond and how good is what you send? The follow-up deck is not seen just by the person you spoke with — it is forwarded to colleagues who were not on the call and must sell MOTM to people who have never met you. A strong deck covers: capabilities, relevant case studies, credibility proof, and contact information.
questions_to_ask: Does our capability deck reflect the specific conversation we just had — or is it generic?
Does it include the most relevant case study for this prospect type?
Is it something the prospect could forward to their MD or CFO and have it speak for itself?
Will it arrive within 24 hours of the conversation?
recommended_action: Have a MOTM capability deck ready to customise within 30 minutes for any prospect conversation. The deck must be clean, professional, and tailored — referencing specific points from the conversation, including the most relevant MOTM case, and arriving with a personal covering note within 24 hours.
what_not_to_do: Do not send a generic company brochure three days after a conversation — this signals low responsiveness and low professionalism. Do not send a deck that could have been sent to any prospect without modification — tailoring signals genuine interest in their specific situation. Do not make the deck too long — the prospect and their colleagues need to be able to read it in 10 minutes.
motm_application: MOTM must have a professional capability deck that can be quickly customised for each prospect — reflecting their industry, their challenge, and the most relevant MOTM case. The covering note should reference at least two specific things discussed in the conversation. A generic deck sent late is a BD failure disguised as a BD follow-up.

principle_name: Do Not Pre-Qualify Too Aggressively — No One Has Budget for Something They Have Not Decided to Buy
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: When deciding whether to pursue a prospect who does not have obvious immediate budget or who is below the usual decision-making level. The correct question to ask about early-stage prospects is under what conditions would they be able to act — not can they buy today.
when_not_to_use: If a prospect is clearly in the wrong type of company or a completely irrelevant industry, that is a genuine fit issue — not a pre-qualification issue. Reserve BD effort for prospects in the right company type regardless of their current budget status.
principle: Ruthlessly eliminating prospects who do not currently have obvious budget or authority is a mistake in professional services. No one has budget today for a service they have not yet decided to buy. Budget is created when a compelling case is made — capital finds high-return opportunities. A wide, patient net in the early stages beats a narrow, aggressive pre-qualification screen that eliminates prospects who will have budget once the case is built.
questions_to_ask: Under what conditions would this become a priority for you?
What would need to change in your business for this kind of investment to make sense?
Is there a planning cycle or budget review coming up where this could be considered?
If the ROI case were compelling, what would the approval process look like?
recommended_action: Engage with any prospect who is in the right type of company and role, even without obvious immediate budget. Use early engagement to understand their situation and build the ROI case that creates budget. Invest more heavily in prospects who are in the right company type and at a senior enough level — even if budget is not yet confirmed.
what_not_to_do: Do not dismiss a prospect because they initially say they do not have budget — budget follows a compelling case. Do not eliminate a junior contact just because they cannot approve the engagement — they may be the internal champion who brings the decision maker into the conversation. Do not spend months with a prospect who is clearly in the wrong type of company.
motm_application: MOTM BD should not dismiss a prospect who says they do not have budget for sales outsourcing. Budget follows a compelling case. The job in early conversations is to build the ROI case and establish the relationship — not to confirm that budget already exists. A prospect who says there is no budget today may create budget next quarter if the case is compelling and the relationship is strong.

principle_name: Stay In Touch When Contacts Change Companies — Trust Is Portable
author: Tom McMakin & Doug Fletcher
when_to_use: When a key contact at a prospect or existing client company announces they are leaving or moving to a new role. This is one of the highest-ROI BD moments that most BD people completely miss.
when_not_to_use: Do not immediately pitch when a contact changes company — give the relationship time to re-establish in the new context before introducing a commercial conversation. The goal is to maintain the relationship, not to immediately monetise the move.
principle: When a prospect or client contact moves to a new company, the trust they have in you moves with them. They carry the relationship — the credibility, the familiarity, the positive associations — to their new role. Staying in touch with contacts when they change roles — even helping them with their job search or their transition if appropriate — builds extraordinary loyalty and often opens doors to a completely new company and a new BD opportunity without any cold outreach.
questions_to_ask: Have we congratulated this contact on their new role?
Is there anything we can do to help them succeed in their new position?
Is their new company a potential MOTM prospect?
How long should we wait before introducing a commercial conversation with them in their new role?
recommended_action: When a key contact changes companies, proactively reach out to congratulate them and ask about their new role. Stay in contact through the transition. After they have settled in — typically 60-90 days — ask about their new context and whether any of the challenges they faced at their previous company are present in the new one.
what_not_to_do: Do not lose track of a warm contact when they leave a company and have to start from zero with a cold approach to their new employer. Do not immediately pitch when a contact moves — let the relationship re-establish first. Do not treat the relationship as belonging to the company rather than the person.
motm_application: MOTM BD should actively track when contacts at prospect or client companies change roles and proactively reach out to congratulate them. A warm contact who trusted MOTM at their previous company carries that trust to their new employer — and is worth more than any cold approach to that same company. One relationship maintained through a job change can open two companies instead of one.
